title: Katagiri Roshi's Peaceful Life
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The teacher encourages the audience to question their assumptions about what it means to be part of a community and how continuity is defined, highlighting that practice can take many forms and that commitment to the path is not limited by external circumstances or expectations. The importance of embracing uncertainty and living in vow, or making a commitment to practice despite any perceived limitations, is emphasized through Katagiri Roshi's teachings on Right View and the Buddha's way. This approach involves cultivating humility, openness, and trust, rather than striving for achievement or perfection.

sentences.text: Thank you again for being here.
It would be totally possible to take it for granted.
If you came down here on a Thursday night, there would be a bunch of really nice Zen students here.
That's a total assumption, right?
What if none of us came?
It's so wonderful.
I know we can't all come all the time, so we do have this broad community to help make sure we continue to have this opportunity to practice together, but it's a good thing to just check yourself on.
Oh, someone will be there.
There's a lot we assume, right?
We assume a certain kind of continuity in life, and it's an assumption.
So that ties into the topic of tonight.
I want to return to an exploration of Right View, the first of the Eightfold Path of the Buddha.
How do we view things?
How do we perceive things?
How do we assume things to be?
How do we view reality?
We don't always notice, because we just think that our view is reality.
How do we view ourselves and others?
Similar.
We don't always notice, because we just think, I know who I am, and I've got you figured out.
How do we view the many branches and turnings and opportunities on the path of life that lie before us?
Some of those we see, probably many of them we don't see.
And they use this word, right, which is a little bit tricky.
It's not exactly right instead of wrong.
More like right meaning most helpful or closest or most wholesome.
So maybe Right View is the understanding or the feeling for the world that's closer, closer to how things are, less limited by our blinders and confusion and self-centeredness.
Because the problem, of course, is that any view is still a view, and no view is completely right.
And neither is any view completely wrong.
This whole topic is a little beyond right and wrong.
So, a pointer to Right View that I've really been appreciating lately, and we've been exploring it a little bit in the weekday morning sit.
We're on Zoom at 7 on the weekday mornings.
Another time I always assume someone will be there, and it's been pretty great for a couple of years.
I click on the little Zoom thing and 12, 15 people's little faces appear.
It's amazing.
So lately I've been sharing a poem by Katagiri Roshi.
I want to share that poem here and explore it a little bit and share with you a little bit about who he was.
Now you're all settled, but for this I need a couple people to help me pass things out.
I brought you a copy.
Thanks.
By the way, I was also a little while ago exploring and viewing this interesting little ritual where the 50-something white guy gets waited on by these wonderful women.
It's kind of strange, but thank you.
They got me water and my seat and helped me.
It's wonderful.
What a blessing.
And I only hope I'll have enough opportunities to serve in exchange.
I'll just read this out loud, and you can read along with your eyes if you like, or just listen.
But now just know that you have a copy of this.
*Being told that it's impossible, one believes in despair.* Is that so?
*Being told that it is possible, one believes in excitement.* That's right.
*But whichever is chosen, it doesn't fit one's heart neatly.
Being asked what is unfitting, I don't know what it is.
But my heart knows somehow.
I feel an irresistible desire to know.
What a mystery a human is.
As to this mystery, clarifying, knowing how to live, knowing how to walk with people, demonstrating and teaching, this is the Buddha.
From my human eyes, I feel it is impossible, really impossible to become Buddha.
But this I, regarding what the Buddha does, vows to practice, to aspire, to be resolute, and tells myself, yes I will, just practice right here now, and achieve continuity, endlessly, forever.
This is living in vow.
Herein is one's peaceful life found.*
Excuse me one second, I forgot to share this with Robin and Scott on the Zoom, so I'll put it in the chat here for you.
I think you have to click that, maybe, to make it bigger.
This is written by a Zen priest in our lineage named Dainin Katagiri.
He was born in 1926 in Japan, in a priestly family, which most Zen priests were by then, in a family of other Zen priests.
Not all of them were really that super into practice in the way we think about it, but he really was, some were.
He did the full training that was available to him then.
He spent three years at Eiheiji Monastery doing their full-time practice schedule.
And he took a degree at the Soto Zen university called [unclear: "Kamazawa"].
He must have studied English and been somehow connected to the international division of the Soto Zen Church.
Because in 1963, when he was about late 20s, 29, he was sent to Zenshuji, which is the Soto Zen temple in Los Angeles, which I think is the oldest Soto Zen temple in America, founded there in 1922.
There were Soto Zen missionaries way further back, 1860s, 1870s, but maybe they didn't establish temples that lasted.
I'm giving you a little backstory here.
One thing I think is important to realize when you think about Zen history is that we tend to think about Zen in America from a Western convert lens, us being Western converts.
We think about Beat Zen and Alan Watts and Gary Snyder and the first Japanese teachers who came, as if they came to serve Westerners.
But actually that's not the case.
The first Japanese Zen teachers were sent here by the Soto Zen Church to serve the Japanese community.
Just like with any religion, you have a bunch of people who practice and you need a priest.
And then this strange thing started happening in the 50s and 60s.
This is a little bit pre-shadowed by earlier Western people interested in Zen, but in the 50s and 60s there started being this dual-track thing happening.
Sometimes the very same Soto Zen priests would be working in both worlds, which was the case with Suzuki Roshi, the founder of our lineage.
He was sent to San Francisco a few years before.
Katagiri Roshi was sent to Los Angeles for the purpose of taking care of the Japanese people in Japantown in San Francisco.
He was interested in Americans and English.
They both were, both of these men.
But that's not really why he was here.
It just worked out that way.
So it's good to remember that we're only a little part of the story.
It would be a little arrogant and maybe a little racist of us to think otherwise.

The Soto Zen ethnic church reads a little more like what we think of as a church: a place for community, a place for connection, where your babies are blessed and your lost ones are celebrated and mourned.
A place where you can access the spiritual life and a place to be deeply together.
Many Japanese adherents of Zen do practice a little bit of meditation, but it's usually not the main thing.
The main thing is more like going to church in the Christian tradition, and practicing at home, altars at home, chants at home, and so on.
This has been happening in America, as I mentioned, since the 1870s or so, as Japanese immigrants came.
And all this was especially crucial in the 1940s when people of Japanese descent were imprisoned, were interned during World War II.
Such a shameful part of our American history, which I imagine is no longer taught in history class in Florida, I would suspect.
It's probably been avoided like everything else.
But that's a side note.
Excuse me for that.
I just saw another article about all the textbooks they're rejecting and so on and so forth.
But anyway, back to the internment.
Japanese Zen and Pure Land and other priests were also interned.
So they set up ad hoc churches in the housing buildings.
At these internment camps, they didn't even build churches for them.
They didn't even build temple spaces.
So they held their temples in the rooms that they shared in the housing.
But then the fascinating thing about the Western interest in Zen is we wanted to do our own version of what the priests did in their training.
It's very different.
We want to do zazen, and we're interested in enlightenment and all this exciting stuff.
And at first, not super interested in regular community, although I think now we've become more and more interested in community and understand Sangha a little better.
But the first Americans in communities were a little more like meditation boot camp than like what we would recognize as a warm community.
A little intense, not always so warm.
So it's fascinating.
And Katagiri Roshi was very much a part of this history, along with Suzuki Roshi.
Especially because after a few years in L.A., serving the Japanese congregation there, he was sent to San Francisco to help Suzuki Roshi with the Japanese congregation in San Francisco.
But we know what happens then.
The hippies start showing up, and this dual thing starts happening with Western students who probably had to be asked to wash their feet, but were also very serious about meditation.
I don't think either man ever had the idea, I'm going to start a whole new kind of Western Zen.
But it grew up around them, and like good practitioners, they responded.
They responded wholeheartedly with a lot of energy.
They worked really hard, and a lot of love, and a lot of fascination.
I think they were really fascinated.
Like, wow, these Americans are really interesting.
I wonder what they said to each other in Japanese.
Did you see that?
Did you really do that?
Okay.

Eventually, both of them, I'm not sure exactly how this happened, it doesn't seem like anyone talks about it, but somehow they became disconnected from their responsibilities with the Soto Zen Church, and were just focusing on the Americanized Zen centers they helped found.

Katagiri Roshi was particularly helpful to Suzuki Roshi at Tassajara, which was the first American Zen monastery, where they really wanted to do things as fully and completely according to the model that they had learned at Eiheiji in Japan.
But Katagiri had been to Eiheiji a year and a half longer than Suzuki Roshi, and several years more recently, so he remembered the form a lot better, so he worked on it.
They also brought up another priest, I forget his name, great big guy, that really was kind of a drill sergeant, Kanagawa, or Katagawa or something.
They were working together to help these young American Zen students really embody the feeling of practice and learn about it.
Eventually, I think Katagiri Roshi wanted a little more space than just being Suzuki Roshi's second.

People started appreciating him and asking him to teach, and I don't know where I heard this from, but I heard this story that one time Katagiri was flying from San Francisco to New York, an American Zen student sitting next to him.
San Francisco, L.A. and New York were pretty much the only places in the 60s and 70s that you could do this Western style of Zen.
It wasn't really available anywhere else.
Somewhere about the middle of the flight, he looked out the window and pointed and asked his student in the next seat, are there Zen centers down there?
And the student said, oh, God, no, that's the Midwest. [unclear: "I don't do that there"].
And [unclear: "the seat was planted"].
Katagiri thought, oh, that's where I need to go.
Then strangely, he was soon after invited to Minneapolis to teach by some early Zen students in Minneapolis who had seen this scene in San Francisco, and they invited him there.
He went and ended up staying, and founded a center called Minnesota Zen Meditation Center in 1972, which is just a year after Suzuki Roshi died, 1971.
Now, meanwhile, back in San Francisco, so he's in Minneapolis, establishing this center, and people are coming to practice, and little by little, just like happened here, little by little.
In the meantime, in San Francisco, Suzuki Roshi only had time before he died.
He had a pretty sudden onset of liver cancer, I think was the cancer.
So he only completed the full ritual of Dharma transmission with one student.
And back then, too, it was really a big deal.
Teachers, Roshis, were held in very high esteem, put on tall pedestals.

So it was a big deal that only one person in the community received transmission, and therefore this person, Dick Baker, Richard Baker, was absolutely going to go on to be the new abbot and be in charge of everything.
Dick Baker was a larger-than-life personality, so well-suited to jumping up on top of the pedestal.
And also a very brilliant guy, a very good teacher.
I've met many of his direct students over the years.
They always talk about how Baker Roshi could just tell them the thing they needed to hear or challenge them in just the right way, and very insightful.
He could really call things well.
He was also incredibly effective as an organizational leader and a fundraiser and a builder.
He got these incredible deals on real estate that then became Tassajara and Green Gulch Farm and raised a gazillion dollars.
And people were blown away by him.
And I think, like many men, when a lot of people are blown away with you, you end up being pretty blown away with yourself after a while.
But everyone says he was quite brilliant.
When he was at Green Gulch during those times, at each center he would have an attendant.
His attendant at Green Gulch Farm was a then-student named Norman Fisher.

But eventually it came out in the 1980s that it had really gotten to his head: Baker Roshi had been sleeping with students, bending all kinds of rules, insisting on all kinds of things that somehow made sense to everybody at the time.
Once they snapped out of it and looked around, it really seemed a bit much, a bit lavish.
Like he had a fancy BMW with a driver, because he was constantly moving between the three centers that they had in San Francisco, which are a few hours apart.
One of the funny things I remember hearing was, he was the main teacher for the whole place, all three centers.
He was the teacher.
So he was always in motion, showing up, giving a talk, giving dokasan, leading a retreat, then on to the next place.
He worked hard, as far as I can tell.
One of the funny things was he needed to have a library.
This was pre-Internet.
So he could do all this teaching and write all these talks, what he insisted on is he needed to have three identical libraries.
Whenever a new book of interest came out, and there weren't that many books in English on Buddhism then, three copies would be ordered.
A copy would be delivered to each of the three libraries, put on the exact same shelf in the exact same order, so that wherever he was, he could just reach up and know exactly where the book is.
Anyway, then the shit hit the fan in 1983-84, and it became public, especially that he was sleeping with the wife of an important friend and donor of the Zen Center.
He'd made advances on other women and just really had some boundary issues, that's for sure.
That's one of the downsides of having the lofty teacher: people don't question anything until it hits the fan, and then they question everything.
So it created a huge confusion.
People stopped sitting.
I remember hearing that the Zendo at Green Gulch was pretty much empty for about a year.
That's shocking to everybody.
They were just wounded and hurt in a big way.
That their teacher, who represented Suzuki Roshi to them, who everybody loved, who represented Buddha, could do such a thing.
Eventually he was forced to resign.
And also, as a result, the Zen Center reorganized.
It turned out the board had been barely a rubber stamp, and here he was running absolutely everything.
The way Norman used to talk about it was something like this.
Dick.
He called him Dick.
Norman's kind of allergic to titles.
He never uses people's titles, except maybe the Dalai Lama.
I remember him telling me, yeah, Dick worked really hard, and he was really effective, and he really felt like he needed a lot, and he did.
He needed the libraries.
He needed lots of assistance.
He needed the car.
And eventually he needed lots of girlfriends, too.
I don't think Norman meant to let him off the hook with it exactly, but Norman had watched all this, and it made sense to him how Baker Roshi had worked himself into this unethical corner.

He worked himself in so thoroughly that he remained convinced for years, and maybe he still is convinced, I don't know, that he really hadn't done anything wrong, and the whole thing was a big misunderstanding.

I remember hearing, I was at Tassajara, and the previous year he had come there the first time since this big blowout, and the thing they said was, it was wonderful to see him, and it was really weird, because it was really clear he still doesn't get it.
He still doesn't understand what happened here.
Delusions are boundless, as we say.
And someone can be that deluded and be a wonderful teacher, too, for sure.
It's very strange.
Anyway, after all that happened, San Francisco Zen Center needed the guidance.
They had this single teacher model, this high and lofty model, which they were trying to reinvent, but it takes time.
They hadn't really empowered other students to be teachers.
Norman talks about this a lot, too.
He says, if this hadn't happened, and so many people hadn't left, and they hadn't reshuffled everything, he would not be a teacher today, he feels.
So it was created by this situation, that then there was room for other people to come forward and have more like a community of teachers, like we try to do here.
But anyway, in 1985, they realized we need help, and they called on Katagiri Roshi, and he came.
That's where I met him in 1986.
He was in and out of Zen Center, I think, for the second half of the 80s.
I did my first practice period at Green Gulch as a young man in the fall of 1986.
He was the teacher.
He wasn't there all the time.
He would appear and disappear, which I figure now must be he went home to Minnesota to see his family.
He had young children then, I think.
Yeah, he would have.
But he was there.
He was the leader.
He taught a class.
I'd see him on the paths, walking and bowing.
He was the teacher for the seven-day Rohatsu sesshin that concluded my eight weeks of training at Green Gulch.
He was a small man, like many Japanese people.
But when he walked and bowed and stood and sat, it was just with a certain kind of solidity.
There was something to it, some kind of power.
And maybe some of that was my projection, probably.
He's the only Japanese teacher around, so, like, wow.
But some of it, I think, was very true, deep in his lived practice his whole life.
Here's what his student, Zuiko Redding, says of him:
*My basic memory of Katagiri is how he paid total attention to what was in front of him.
He took care of each thing as if it were the most important thing in the world, whether it was throwing away the trash or talking to another person.
He really listened and tried to give the best answer he knew how to give.
He also encouraged each of us to stand up in our own space and follow our own wisdom rather than depending on him for answers or affirmation.*

*I would sometimes tell him exactly what I thought about some idea I had, disagreeing with him, only to turn and see him smiling at me with a big, broad smile, glad that I wasn't buying into his agenda.*
Big-hearted guy.
His English was never super great, a thick accent to the end of his life.
And he had some very short phrases he used a lot.
I remember him saying a lot of times, this was before Nike stole it from him, he would say, "Just do it!"

And also in that sesshin, there was a full moon during the sesshin, and we were in this basement zendo at San Francisco Zen Center, so it was just these little windows that were actually at the street level, but occasionally you could see the moon through these little windows.
Every night when he would see it, it was the first time I think I'd ever heard anybody speaking during Zazen, which was very strictly silent.
He said something like, "Full moon in the autumn sky."
And we just all shivered.
I'll never forget that.
Full moon.

Anyway, this was a sesshin I talk about sometimes, my first sesshin, where I, as a young, eager guy, and I think part of it too was the way Zen was presented back then, a little more of an emphasis on its intensity and power.
So I absorbed all that like a sponge, and I was trying so hard.
Gave myself all kinds of intense physical pain, terrible back-outs, backaches.
I didn't quite make it to back-outs.
Not that bad.
Backaches, yeah.
And I was pressing my eyes so hard without knowing it that I created the little floaty things you can get if you press your eyes.
I did that from the inside somehow.
That was weird.
And I was just exhausted.
Getting through the day was almost impossible.
And there were pretty full days. 4 a.m. wake-up probably.
Bed at 9, 9:30.
It's also the one where I foolishly counted on the schedule how many Zazen periods there were, and I would count them down.
The number did not go down very quickly, I can tell you that.
Yeah, don't do that, it's bad.
Norman was there also.
He had not yet received Dharma transmission, so I remember I went to him at least once for practice discussion.
He did help convince me to relax a little bit, by changing the subject and talking about breath.
That helped me relax a little bit.
And when I did actually manage to relax a little bit, there was this incredible rush of energy and relief.
It was just like...
And I felt suddenly really good, like really good.
Like so happy.
And Zazen briefly got a little easier.
Just because I was not making it so hard, basically.
I'd assisted a little on making things hard.
And that was when my time to see Katagiri Roshi in Doksan came up.
It was a dark room. [unclear: "Ben was of short meeting"].
I told him about this feeling, and he was very sweet.
He said something like, "Many kinds of enlightenment experience.
Maybe there's some small enlightenment.
Very nice.
Please practice."
Rang his little bell.
Off I went.
He didn't tell me, yeah, you were just a little wound up there.
Relax, dude.
Katagiri also gave really long Dharma talks.
Like really long.
Lately, maybe you've noticed, I've been trying to give shorter Dharma talks.
I've actually been a little bit successful at that.
There's time for discussion and stuff.
But tonight's an homage to Katagiri Roshi, so I think I can't do that.
It has to be a longer talk.
His talks were at least 90 minutes, maybe longer.
There's a strong sense back then of don't move.
I remember being surrounded by the senior students of the center sitting apparently in full lotus, very good posture, not budging for the whole time.
I don't know how their knees didn't fall off.
I would, of course, try my best to emulate them.

I remember after [unclear: "Sashino's"] back at Green Gulch, one of the senior people there who went on to become a teacher for a few of us, Blanche Hartman, asked me about, she wasn't there, so she asked me, "What did Roshi talk about?"
I had no idea.
I couldn't remember a thing.
It was so embarrassing to say to her.
I'm not sure.
But she smiled.
I think she understood how it had been for me.
And probably my most important memory of Katagiri Roshi is not like I really knew him or spent much time with him, but interestingly, this feels like my most important memory of him.
I was doing my temple cleaning job, Soji, and I was in one of the hallways.
I was wiping down the baseboards, pretty big building, San Francisco Zen Center, lots of dusty baseboards.
Zen is famous for hyper cleaning.
We haven't been doing that practice as much here, but we should.
Anyway, I ended up by his room, apparently, because there was Katagiri Roshi in the hallway by an open door talking with another Japanese man I didn't know, in Japanese.
I'm not sure why this felt so deep and meaningful to me.
Of course, I didn't understand what they were saying.
But something about the energy between them, something about the attentiveness and connectedness in their conversation, somehow just deeply caring, intimate, and a feeling of sadness, too.
There's a feeling of sadness in the body language, in the words.
So something really poignant.
And Katagiri Roshi's legacy is similar to Suzuki Roshi's: hanging in there for decades and creating a center and training people and being there for them day after day after day after day.
Many strong American Zen teachers emerged from Minnesota.
I've had the pleasure to meet some of them.
And most of the authors in that book, On the Eightfold Path by the American Zen Woman, those are almost all Katagiri Roshi students.
As is, not a direct student, our dear friend and colleague Jeff Kelly, who is from the Katagiri lineage, who was a Katagiri student.
And so is Ben Connolly, a student of Tim Burkett, who gets mixed up with me a lot, as you could understand.
Usually it's exactly like what happened to me one time in second grade.
In second grade there were three Tims.
And Tim Nolan was the popular Tim.
And one time the cutest girl in class looked across the room and said, "Tim!"
And of course she was not talking to me.
She was talking to Tim Nolan.
And then 40 years later I go to this Zen teachers meeting and someone says to me, "Tim, Tim Burkett, I'm so glad you're here.
I've so appreciated your teachings."
And I said, "Ah, that's not me."
And also Judith Ragier, who we got to see on Zoom talking about her powerful journey of healing and her wonderful book about untangling karma.
So these are all Katagiri Roshi disciples.
And Ben Connolly will be in this seat next week, so be here if you can, talking about his new book on our old buddy Vasubandhu.
That part about the three realities that I could never quite figure out.
We'll see if Ben has it figured out.
He's good at writing books, that's for sure.
But Katagiri Roshi's legacy sadly is not unblemished.
Here's what it says at the top of the ethics webpage on the Minnesota Zen Meditation Center website.
This is sad.
*Many years ago, Minnesota Zen Meditation Center faced an extremely serious ethical issue.

Several years after the 1990 death of our beloved founder, Dainian Katagiri Roshi, we were shocked and deeply saddened to hear that he had engaged in sexual relationships with at least two women who were his students and made unwelcome advances to some others.
In response, we took careful and thoughtful steps to prevent anything like this from ever happening again at MZMC.
We instituted a clear code of ethics stating that any sexual relationships between a teacher and his or her student is inappropriate and unacceptable.
We developed teacher training programs and a leadership structure designed to support a safe and transparent environment.
All MZMC teachers have received training and the ethical standards expected of them and have wholeheartedly and without reservation agreed to live by these standards.*
And then the page goes on to explain their ethical program and their precepts.
So this came out after he died.
Another well-known student of Katagiri Roshi's is the writer and teacher Natalie Goldberg.
This is kind of wild.
Before this came out, she wrote one book about how much she loved and treasured her work and her training and her practice with Katagiri.
And then after this came out, she realized, "I've got to write another book now," and she did.
She wrote another book about betrayal and failure.
And this poem also was discovered posthumously after his death, so I can only assume that he wrote it for himself, you know?
That he wrote it for himself to encourage himself, to explore for himself what this is, this thing he'd already been doing by then for 50 years at least.
Norman also really appreciated this poem.
He used to have his pre-students read it at the beginning of meetings, which is how I first learned of it, but I've always appreciated it.
And lately it's really come up again for me.
So let's explore a little bit here in the time we have left.
*Being told that it's impossible, one believes in despair.*
Is that so?
*Being told that it is possible, one believes in excitement.*
That's right.
So if we really think about life, it's impossible, right?
I mean, it's not going to end well, right?
It's impossible.
We'll never quite make sense of it.
We'll never quite be clear on who we are or what's going on.
We'll never be sure of anything, actually.
And when we do think we're sure, we sooner or later find out we were wrong or a little off or really upside down.
And so if we approach life with the idea that we can somehow figure it out and make it understandable and clear and do it right, it's just not going to work.
So how could there not be a little despair about that in us?
It's only natural, it's only logical.
Is that so?
Oh man, hard.

And yet, if we just take everything one step at a time, one breath at a time, trust the situation, trust each other, trust the practice, meet each other, bow, sit, listen, speak from the heart, if we practice kindness, if we love each other, it works out perfectly.
Is there really a problem here?
Wonderful.
One believes in excitement.
That's right.
*And yet, neither seems to be quite right either.
Right.
Neither is a complete view.
Whichever is chosen, it does not fit one's heart neatly.*
It's not this or that, or neither.
So maybe life is impossible and possible somehow at the same time in a way that we can never quite fit in our heads.
But maybe it fits in our hearts, at least almost.
Isn't that an interesting phrase?
He said it does not quite fit neatly.
*Being asked what is unfitting, I don't know.
I don't know what it is.
But my heart knows somehow.*
I so appreciate the humility of this, you know.
It's advanced practitioner and teacher, beloved person: "I don't know."
But somehow, there's something here.
And our way is this way, right?
Our way is, Suzuki Roshi said, "not always so."
The opposite is always included.
Nothing's left out.
Nothing's exclusive.
It's not neither.
It's not either.
It's not this.
So the true reality just can't be diminished into categories like possible or impossible.
Me or you.
How it really is can't be navigated with our heads.
But the heart knows somehow.
*I feel an irresistible desire to know.*
To know what can't be known, right?
What a mystery a human is.
Like, what?
You know?
It probably should be our basic emotion all the time.
Every minute we wake up, we should be like, what?
How is this happening?
I'm alive?
Now what?
It's probably going to be like, whoop-de-do.
Got to get to work.
*As to this mystery, as to this mystery, clarifying, knowing how to live, knowing how to walk with people, demonstrating and teaching, this is the Buddha.
This is the Buddha.*
So it's a together life, a together world, a together practice.
The reason why there's families and communities and villages and sanghas.
And I particularly always love this line about walking with people.
It makes me think of when I was first allowed, or invited, to offer one-on-one meetings at our big retreat at Lad Samish Island Camp, which is this great big spread out place.
There's lots of space between the buildings and these big lawns.
Anyway, the meditation hall was in one big building and one part of the lawn, and the little rooms we used for the interviews were across this wide, expansive lawn in another part.
And I was doing interviews, but I was not yet transmitted, so it was the form that we call practice discussion.
I wasn't just sitting in the room waiting for people to bring me the next person.
The form was that I would walk across the lawn and get the next person, and we would walk together to the room where we would meet.
I really treasured those walks, you know?
Sometimes I would feel nervous or feel one way or the other about it or feel something, but I could always appreciate the power of that walking together.
